<title>explain: missing-blob probe lazy-fetches per blob, hammering mirrors with bogus wants</title>
<description>
> Agent-generated issue. Verify facts against source. Treat proposed solutions, recommendations, and agent-made decisions as hypotheses, not settled direction.

Repo: `entireio/cli`

## Observed facts

* On 2026-08-26 ~21:42–22:12 UTC, `entire explain --checkpoint 01M07BGK52MB63Y83A0RVYQB2N --json` runs (invoked by a codex agent session in a local `entireio/cli` clone) produced **1,805 single-want** `git-upload-pack` **requests** against the `entire://aws-us-east-2` mirrors of `entireio/cli` and `entireio/cli-checkpoints`, all answered `503`. entiredb's shadow classifier tagged 100% of them `verdict:bogus` (objects the repos never contained). The resulting 17–38% error rate on the git-protocol route tripped the availability SLO fast burn and paged P1 ([incident.io](<http://incident.io>) INC-78, Datadog monitor 313962708-family). ap-southeast-2 was paged ~21h earlier by the same server-side class (INC-74).
* Mechanism, verified in source: `prefetchCheckpointBlobs` (`cmd/entire/cli/explain.go:902`) is designed to collect missing blobs and fetch them "in a single `git fetch-pack` invocation per store". But the collection step, `FetchingTree.CollectMissingBlobs` → `blobOnDisk` (`cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/fetching_tree.go:211`), probes each blob with a bare `git cat-file -e <hash>`. In a `blob:none` partial clone with promisor remotes, `cat-file -e` on an absent object triggers git's internal lazy fetch — one single-want upload-pack request **per configured promisor remote** — before reporting the blob missing. The batching never gets a chance.
* Each failed probe costs ~1s (remote-helper spawn + discovery per attempt, plus node failover inside the helper), so ~900 probed blobs took two ~14-minute grinds while the user-facing command sat on a spinner. Repo-local `.entire/logs/entire.log` shows the prefetch failing (`explain prefetch: cp subtree not found`, 14:46:17 and 14:56:46 -07:00) and per-file fallback reads >1s apart.
* Trigger condition: a checkpoint referenced by a commit trailer whose blobs exist only in local refs (never pushed), so every probe is a guaranteed miss on both mirrors. Any repo with the standard two entire promisor remotes doubles the requests.
* Server-side amplification (separate issue, <issue id="99c35963-dd1b-4bf4-a691-66c80401f30e" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-1939/decide-whether-to-flip-the-missing-want-503-default">ENT-1939</issue>): entiredb answers never-existed wants with `503 + Retry-After: 5` instead of a terminal 40x, so these client misses count against the git-protocol availability SLO.

## Proposed approach

Set `GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1` (or `--no-lazy-fetch`) on the `git cat-file -e` probe in `blobOnDisk` so the missing-blob analysis is a pure local check and the prefetch batches as designed. Audit the other `git cat-file` call sites in `fetching_tree.go` (`readFileViaGit`, the per-File fallback path) for the same hazard — the per-File fallback may *intentionally* fetch, but it should fetch once per blob, not probe-fetch during analysis.

## Alternatives

* Client-side negative caching / early abort after N consecutive missing-blob fetch failures in one explain run (bounds the damage but keeps the per-blob probes).
* Rely solely on the server fix (<issue id="99c35963-dd1b-4bf4-a691-66c80401f30e" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-1939/decide-whether-to-flip-the-missing-want-503-default">ENT-1939</issue> terminal 40x): stops the SLO burn but keeps explain slow (~1s per missing blob) and keeps the request storm.

## Open questions

* Should the per-File fallback fetcher also stop attempting remote fetches for blobs already classified missing by the prefetch analysis in the same run?
* `GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH` requires git ≥ 2.43; confirm the CLI's minimum supported git version or use `cat-file --no-lazy-fetch` / batch `cat-file --batch-check` with the env var accordingly.
</description>

## My read of the task

- **Problem:** The missing-blob analysis calls `git cat-file` once per blob. In partial clones, both the `-e` probe and the pre-fetch `-p` read can silently contact promisor remotes.
- **Goal:** Keep missing-blob analysis local so `PreFetch` remains the only network operation and batches all missing hashes.
- **Non-goal:** Server handling of nonexistent wants remains ENT-1939.
- **Verified source evidence:** [`CollectMissingBlobs`](/Users/pfleidi/entire/cli/.entire/worktrees/pfleidi-ent-1989-explain-missing-blob-probe-lazy-fetches-per-blob-hammering/cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/fetching_tree.go:181) reaches `cat-file -e`; [`File`](/Users/pfleidi/entire/cli/.entire/worktrees/pfleidi-ent-1989-explain-missing-blob-probe-lazy-fetches-per-blob-hammering/cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/fetching_tree.go:105) runs `cat-file -p` before its explicit fetcher.
- **Recorded intent:** The introducing checkpoint says those calls should detect already-local blobs and avoid network fetches. It also shows an efficiency review dismissed batching based on an assumption of roughly five blobs; the incident’s ~900-blob case invalidates that assumption.
- **Still unverified:** I haven’t independently accessed the incident telemetry or reproduced the storm against a synthetic promisor remote.

## Assumptions to challenge

- The issue says this facility requires Git 2.43. Official Git history places client-side `--no-lazy-fetch` and the equivalent environment behavior in Git 2.45, not 2.43. [Git 2.45 release notes](https://github.com/git/git/blob/master/Documentation/RelNotes/2.45.0.adoc), [current Git documentation](https://git-scm.com/docs/git).
- I found no declared minimum Git version in this repository. On older clients, the environment variable is ignored, leaving the bug intact.

## Options I see

- **Set `GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1` on both `cat-file` calls.** Smallest change, trivial rollback, and preserves the existing design on Git 2.45+. It still launches one local process per candidate and doesn’t protect older Git.
- **Also batch the analysis through one `cat-file --batch-check`.** Removes the per-blob process count as well as remote traffic. It adds output parsing and more test surface; the incident measures remote latency, not local subprocess time.
- **Design pre-2.45 protection or establish Git 2.45 as the minimum.** This broadens the task into compatibility policy because older Git lacks a reliable local-only `cat-file` boundary.

My recommendation is the first option, applied to both `-e` and `-p`, unless protecting Git older than 2.45 is required. Batching can remain out of scope until local-only subprocess time is measured.

## Validation plan

### Automated tests

- Build a synthetic partial clone with a local promisor remote.
- Verify missing-blob collection doesn’t hydrate blobs or contact the remote.
- Verify `File` invokes the injected fetcher exactly once rather than lazy-fetching first.
- Preserve the stale go-git index case: a blob already on disk must still be readable without invoking the fetcher.

### Local validation

Run the focused checkpoint package test and use Git tracing against the synthetic remote to verify no upload-pack process starts during analysis.

### Staging validation

From a fresh partial clone containing a valid pushed checkpoint:

```bash
git clone --filter=blob:none <staging-repo-url> <directory>
cd <directory>
entire checkpoint explain --checkpoint <pushed-checkpoint-id> --json --no-pager
```

Expected: successful output and at most one explicit batch fetch per store, never one request per blob.

### Production validation

Roll out normally and watch the existing git-protocol request/error telemetry and bogus-want classifier. Directly manufacturing an unpushed checkpoint in production is not acceptable.

No. Older Git versions can also trigger the lazy fetch; newer Git didn’t introduce the bug.

The distinction is:

- **Git before 2.45:** `cat-file` can lazy-fetch missing promisor objects, but there’s no general client-side opt-out for this path.
- **Git 2.45+:** behavior remains lazy by default, but Git added `--no-lazy-fetch` and `GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1` to disable it. [Git 2.45 release notes](https://github.com/git/git/blob/master/Documentation/RelNotes/2.45.0.adoc), [Git documentation](https://git-scm.com/docs/git)

Therefore Git 2.43 is vulnerable, and the issue’s “requires Git ≥2.43” statement is incorrect—the proposed fix requires **Git 2.45+**. Newer Git supplies the remedy; it isn’t the cause. Some older maintenance releases recognize the same variable inside server-side `upload-pack`, but that doesn’t protect this client-side `cat-file` call.
Can we implement it in a way that doesn't rely on a git version check? If we're setting GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1 older versions should simply ignore it, no?

Yes. That’s the cleanest approach.

Set `GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1` on both `git cat-file` subprocesses:

- Git 2.45+ honors it, making the checks local-only.
- Older Git ignores the unknown environment variable and preserves today’s behavior.
- Unlike `git --no-lazy-fetch`, it won’t fail on older versions.
- No version detection or compatibility branch is needed.

The limitation is coverage, not compatibility: older Git remains vulnerable to the request storm, but it isn’t broken or regressed. I’d plan around this narrow implementation unless fixing pre-2.45 Git is a requirement.

## Updated alignment

### Problem and goal

Missing-blob discovery must be local-only. Today, both `cat-file -e` and the preliminary `cat-file -p` can lazy-fetch, turning temporary mirror lag into one request per blob and promisor remote.

The goal is to restore the intended boundary:

1. Inspect local availability.
2. Batch-fetch missing blobs explicitly.
3. Retain per-file fetching only as best-effort recovery.

### Recommended scope

- Set `GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1` on both `git cat-file` subprocesses in [`fetching_tree.go`](/Users/pfleidi/entire/cli/.entire/worktrees/pfleidi-ent-1989-explain-missing-blob-probe-lazy-fetches-per-blob-hammering/cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/fetching_tree.go:210).
- Do not add Git version detection.
- Accept that Git before 2.45 ignores the variable and retains current behavior.
- Keep the explicit per-file fetcher. The preliminary `cat-file -p` becomes local-only; if the blob is absent, the configured fetcher gets one deliberate attempt.
- Do not cache the prefetch result or suppress fallback fetches. Prefetch is best-effort, and suppressing fallback would convert recoverable batch failures into immediate read failures.
- Do not introduce `--batch-check` yet. The incident measures remote latency, not local subprocess cost, so batching local probes would add parsing and process plumbing without current evidence.
- Keep mirror synchronization investigation out of this client change.

This is a small, reversible behavior correction with no new abstraction or compatibility branch.

## Validation plan

### Automated test

Extend the existing partial-clone integration coverage in [`explain_test.go`](/Users/pfleidi/entire/cli/.entire/worktrees/pfleidi-ent-1989-explain-missing-blob-probe-lazy-fetches-per-blob-hammering/cmd/entire/cli/integration_test/explain_test.go:326). It already creates:

- A synthetic pushed checkpoint.
- A smart-protocol `file://` remote.
- A `blob:none` fetch with promisor configuration.
- A successful `entire checkpoint explain` run.

Add scoped Git tracing or request instrumentation and assert:

- Missing-blob classification doesn’t initiate remote fetches.
- Explain performs only the deliberate batch fetch needed to hydrate the checkpoint.
- The checkpoint remains readable afterward.

This tests real Git behavior without mocks or production-only seams.

### Local verification

```bash
go test -run TestExplain_CheckpointSucceedsAfterTreelessFetch -count=1 -tags=integration ./cmd/entire/cli/integration_test
go test -count=1 ./cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint
go build ./cmd/entire
mise run lint
```

### Staging

Using an internal test repository configured for filtered fetches and a checkpoint remote:

```bash
entire checkpoint explain --checkpoint <pushed-checkpoint-id> --json --no-pager
```

Expected:

- Explain succeeds.
- At most one deliberate multi-want fetch per relevant store.
- No series of single-want requests during missing-blob analysis.

### Production

Use rollout telemetry only:

- Watch git-protocol request volume and error rate.
- Check that explain runs no longer correlate with bursts of single-want requests.
- Keep the existing SLO and bogus-want classifier as rollback signals.

Do not manufacture mirror lag, damage ref closure, or reuse incident/customer data in staging or production.

## Decision before planning

Do you approve this exact scope—including unchanged behavior on Git before 2.45 and retaining the per-file fallback—so I can write the implementation plan?

Always review changes against `origin/main` directly. Do not use local `main`, `git merge-base`, a PR base branch, or a user-specified alternate base.

|---------|--------|-------|
| User goal | Conversation | One-line summary, or `not provided` |
| Implementation plan | Conversation / docs | One-line summary, or `not provided` |
| Commits | `git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD` | One-line summary of commit intent |
| Changed surface | diff file list | Main packages/files touched |
| Inferred behavior | commits/tests/docs/user text | Intended behavior change, or `diff-only inference` |

- The user's request and any implementation plan, design notes, or acceptance criteria provided in the conversation.
- Branch commit messages from `git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD`.
- The changed-file list and any obvious intended behavior changes inferred from commits, tests, docs, or user-facing text.

Treat this context as the statement of intent. If the conversation and local docs provide no implementation context, say that intent is inferred from the diff and commits only.

If human PR or trail review comments appear in the conversation, treat them as user-owned context, not default autofix work. Present each one separately with the full verbatim text, whether it is relevant to the current code, and the source-backed reason. Do not automatically edit code for it, reply to it, resolve it, dismiss it, or mark it addressed; the user handles human reviewer conversations separately unless they explicitly select a specific comment for agent action afterward.

If implementation plans, issue bodies, PR descriptions, handoff docs, code comments, trail findings, or prior summaries appear to be agent-generated, treat their proposed solutions as hypotheses rather than accepted requirements. Preserve the observed problem and source-backed constraints, but critically evaluate the proposed fix against the current diff, user request, tests, and simplicity rules. Do not classify a change as correct just because it follows an earlier agent decision, and do not classify a different approach as wrong unless it breaks a human-approved requirement or real contract. Do not treat an agent-written design doc or code comment that mentions a risk as proof the risk was accepted.

### Review Mode Triage

Use **lightweight mode** when the diff is limited to docs, plans, specs, ADRs/RFDs, comments-only prose files, or bounded declarative config/metadata where the changed keys are self-contained, non-secret, and understandable from the file plus nearby docs without tracing code.

Examples that usually qualify:

- `*.md`, `docs/**`, `plans/**`, `specs/**`, `rfds/**`, `adrs/**`
- Agent instructions, skill docs, README text, templates, examples, or prose-only policy files
- Formatting-only metadata or config whose effect is limited to local tooling display or editor behavior
- Tool-local or agent/plugin metadata where the changed keys are descriptive labels, trigger text, local preferences, ordering, or display-only defaults

Use **full mode** when the diff includes any code, tests, scripts, migrations, schemas, dependency manifests or locks, CI workflows, deploy/IaC files, generated artifacts, executable examples, or config whose effect requires code tracing. Also use full mode when a config change is small but security-sensitive, changes permissions, affects deploys, auth, networking, secrets, storage, routing, validation, production runtime behavior, or is ambiguous.

Do not trace code only to prove that obviously descriptive metadata is non-runtime. If the file path and changed keys show local/editor/agent/plugin metadata and no risky terms appear, keep lightweight mode. If the diff mixes lightweight and full-mode files, use full mode. If unsure, use full mode and name the file that made the diff ambiguous.

For lightweight mode, skip section 2's simplification and parallel review streams. Go to section 2A.

For full mode, choose the review intensity before launching agents:

- Use **direct full mode** for small, self-contained code diffs where the changed behavior can be understood from focused reads: a few files, modest diff size, clear intent, no shared/public API change, no dependency or lockfile change, no schema/migration/generated-code boundary, no auth/security/concurrency/storage/deploy/runtime-config surface, and no broad test-strategy change.
- Use **parallel full mode** when the diff is broad, security-sensitive, concurrency-heavy, touches public/shared contracts, changes deploy or data boundaries, has unclear intent, or would benefit from independent review lenses.

If unsure, use parallel full mode and name the file or risk that made the diff too ambiguous for direct review.

For direct full mode, go to section 2B. For parallel full mode, continue to section 2.

Use this section only in parallel full mode. If triage selected lightweight mode or direct full mode, do not run `/simplify` or launch these review streams.

Use Claude's configured default model. Run it non-interactively with edit acceptance, no session persistence, and explicit prohibitions against commits and pushes. If it fails or times out after editing files, preserve the current working tree, show the exact failure, and continue; do not guess which edits belong to Claude or attempt a rollback that could remove user work.

The two streams are:

1. The existing Codex specialist lens team.
2. One independent, read-only Claude review.

Then launch the Codex lens agents and start the Claude process in the same orchestration phase. Start both streams before waiting on either one. Use the runtime's background/session mechanism for Claude rather than a blocking foreground command.

### Review Philosophy

Pass these rules to every Codex agent and the Claude reviewer:

- **It is OK to find nothing.** A clean review is a valid outcome. Do NOT manufacture findings to justify the review. Only flag issues you are confident are real problems.
- **Be opinionated and consistent.** If a pattern is acceptable, don't flag it. If you flag something, commit to that position — don't suggest the opposite approach on a re-review.
- **Don't flag trade-offs with no clear winner.** If there are two reasonable approaches and neither is clearly better, don't flag it. The author already made a choice.
- **High confidence only.** Every finding must pass the bar: "I am confident this is a problem, and I can explain specifically what goes wrong if it's not fixed." Vague unease is not a finding.
- **Permission-friendly reads.** Avoid shell pipelines, command separators, subshells, shell variables, and output filters for read-only investigation because they create extra permission prompts and block background review agents. Do not run commands like `git show HEAD:path | sed -n '10,40p'`. Use workspace file range reads, `rg` with path limits, path-scoped `git diff origin/main -- <path>`, or one standalone `git show <rev>:<path>` only when the output is acceptably small.
- **Intent-aware review.** Review changed code against the review context, not against the old behavior alone. Do not classify an intentional behavior change as Required merely because it differs from `origin/main`. A Required finding must either contradict stated intent, break an existing contract that the intent did not change, introduce a concrete bug/security issue, or leave the intended behavior unverified in a way that would likely fail.
- **Agent proposals are provisional.** Handoffs, issues, code comments, and earlier review summaries written by agents can explain why work started, but they do not settle the design. If review feedback or source evidence shows the proposed solution is weak, say so instead of defending the agent's earlier choice. Draft and pre-PR work is cheap to change. "The risk is documented" is not acceptance unless a human approved the tradeoff, a decision record merged, or a real compatibility constraint requires it.

### Agent 1: Security & Adversarial

Review `git diff origin/main` with fresh eyes for:

- **Injection** — command injection, SQL injection, path traversal
- **TOCTOU and race conditions** — check-then-act patterns, concurrent access without synchronization
- **Unvalidated input at system boundaries** — user input, API parameters, external data
- **Auth/authz gaps** — missing permission checks, privilege escalation paths
- **Secrets or credentials** — hardcoded tokens, leaked keys, credentials in code or config

For EACH finding: read the actual source file and trace whether the code path is reachable in production. Discard any finding you cannot confirm with a concrete code reference.

Review `git diff origin/main` for:

- **Logic errors** — off-by-one, wrong comparison, inverted conditions
- **Nil/null handling** — unchecked nil dereferences, missing error checks (especially unchecked errors in Go)
- **Edge cases in concurrency** — goroutine leaks, missing locks, channel misuse, deferred unlock ordering
- **Redundant state** — state that duplicates existing state, cached values that could be derived
- **Production test seams** — mutable function variables, package-wide settings, reset hooks, or exported knobs added only so tests can swap behavior instead of using dependency injection or a higher-scope test
- **Parameter sprawl** — adding new parameters instead of restructuring
- **Leaky abstractions** — exposing internal details, breaking existing abstraction boundaries
- **Stringly-typed code** — using raw strings where constants or typed values already exist in the codebase
- **Test coverage and scope gaps** — changed behavior, edge cases, or error paths not exercised by meaningful tests; tests that prove implementation details instead of behavior; or unit tests used where integration/e2e coverage is the right confidence boundary. Preserve useful fast unit tests: do not flag them as incomplete merely because they skip wiring that integration/e2e tests own. Before recommending integration/e2e coverage, check whether existing integration/e2e tests already cover that boundary; if not, suggest the narrowest additive test at the missing layer rather than converting a broad unit suite.
- **Test helper over-abstraction** — helpers that hide the behavior, expected values, or assertions and make the test harder to understand than a small amount of duplication

### Agent 3: Simplification & De-slop

Use the local `pfleidi:de-slop` skill's slop taxonomy as the source of truth: `skills/pfleidi/skills/de-slop/SKILL.md` ("What Counts as Slop"). Apply its criteria as a detection lens only — find and report slop; do not run de-slop's remediation workflow, create commits, or open a PR.

Review `git diff origin/main` for:

- **Dead code** — unreachable branches, unused functions, struct fields never read, data computed but never used
- **Reinvention** — hand-rolled solutions to problems already solved by the repo, the standard library, or a dependency in use; name the existing mechanism to use instead
- **Code reuse & duplication** — existing utilities and helpers that could replace newly written code; near-duplicate blocks that should be unified
- **Unnecessary abstractions** — wrapper types, indirection, single-caller layers, speculative interfaces/options/configuration/feature flags, or overly defensive fallbacks that mask errors. Same-type/module pass-through delegators count here: functions, methods, properties, components, commands, or modules whose only behavior is calling another function on the same receiver/module with the same inputs plus a constant/default argument. Treat these as especially suspect when they exist to avoid updating callers after adding an argument, option, dependency, or mode; the clearer fix is usually to update the call sites directly. Treat newly added future-proofing as Required when the diff has no current requirement, caller, concrete failure mode, external contract, or measured bottleneck paying for it. A nicer name or avoiding call-site churn is not a current requirement.
- **Premature optimization** — complexity added for performance no one measured; prefer the clear version unless a bottleneck or stated scale requirement was shown. Flag caches, batching, concurrency, retry/fallback layers, pooling, streaming, lazy loading, or generic performance machinery added for "might need it later" reasons.
- **Unnecessary work** — redundant computations, repeated file reads, duplicate API calls, N+1 patterns
- **Missed concurrency** — independent operations run sequentially when there is a measured or stated latency requirement, the current behavior is too slow, and parallel execution can be bounded safely
- **Hot-path bloat** — blocking work added to startup or per-request paths
